context.text: From 303 Diocletian and his colleagues had tried to destroy the Church: churches were pulled down, the Scriptures burned and the clergy imprisoned, and in the end all were ordered to sacrifice. In April 311 the dying Galerius gave way. His edict, issued at Nicomedia, allowed the Christians "again to be Christians, and to establish the places of their religious assemblies", and asked them to pray for the emperors. In the East, however, Maximin Daia soon renewed the persecution.

In the West Constantine marched on Rome against Maxentius. Lactantius writes that he "was directed in a dream to cause the heavenly sign to be delineated on the shields of his soldiers", the monogram of Christ. Eusebius, who heard the story from the emperor himself, tells of a cross of light seen in the sky with the words "Conquer by this". In October 312 the army of Maxentius was routed at the Milvian Bridge, and Maxentius was driven into the Tiber and drowned.

narrative.text: That winter Constantine went to Milan, and his colleague Licinius came there to marry Constantine's sister Constantia. The two emperors agreed on a common policy toward religion. Licinius then marched against Maximin, routed him in Thrace and entered Nicomedia, the city where the persecution had begun. There, in June 313, he had their decision posted in a letter addressed to the governor of a province. It opens:

When we, Constantine and Licinius, emperors, had an interview at Milan, and conferred together with respect to the good and security of the commonweal, it seemed to us that, amongst those things that are profitable to mankind in general, the reverence paid to the Divinity merited our first and chief attention, and that it was proper that the Christians and all others should have liberty to follow that mode of religion which to each of them appeared best; so that that God, who is seated in heaven, might be benign and propitious to us, and to every one under our government.
narrative.source: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 48, tr. W. Fletcher (ANF vol. 7, 1886)

narrative.text: The letter went beyond the grudging pardon of 311. It set aside every condition laid on the Christians in earlier orders: the freedom granted them was "ample and unconditional", and "the open and free exercise of their respective religions is granted to all others, as well as to the Christians." Their places of assembly, and the other property the Christian community held as a body, were to be restored "without money demanded or price claimed", and those who lost them by restoring them could apply to the emperors for compensation.

The text survives twice. Lactantius copied it in Latin into his book On the Deaths of the Persecutors; Eusebius gives a Greek translation in the tenth book of his Church History, where the emperors' wish reads "that whatever heavenly divinity exists may be propitious to us and to all that live under our government." The name Edict of Milan is a convention: the document that has come down is the letter Licinius posted at Nicomedia, setting out what the two emperors had agreed at Milan.

Lactantius closes his book with a reckoning: "from the overthrow of the Church until its restoration, there was a space of ten years and about four months." Maximin, beaten, gave the Christians full freedom in his own lands and ordered their property returned before he died at Tarsus, pursued by Licinius.

significance.text: For the Church the agreement of 313 marks the end of the great persecutions and the turn toward the age of the councils. Those who had been ordered to sacrifice on pain of death were free to worship, to rebuild and to gather, and their churches were given back. Eusebius, who had seen the houses of prayer thrown down, describes what followed:

After this was seen the sight which had been desired and prayed for by us all; feasts of dedication in the cities and consecrations of the newly built houses of prayer took place, bishops assembled, foreigners came together from abroad, mutual love was exhibited between people and people, the members of Christ's body were united in complete harmony.
significance.source: Eusebius, Church History X.3, tr. A. C. McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1, 1890)

significance.text: The same peace brought a question the Church had not faced before: the place of a Christian emperor in its affairs. Within a year Constantine was referring a quarrel among the bishops of Africa to a council at Rome and then to another at Arles in 314, and in 325 he would summon the bishops of the whole Church to Nicaea.

consequences.text: Licinius later broke with Constantine and, as Socrates and Eusebius record, turned against the Christians of his own lands, forbidding the bishops to visit the pagans and harassing the faithful. Constantine defeated him in 324 near Chrysopolis and became sole emperor, and the next year he called the council of Nicaea.

uncertainty: No text of the agreement made at Milan itself survives. Both versions give the letter as it was published afterwards, and Lactantius dates the posting at Nicomedia to the ides of June in the third consulship of Constantine and Licinius, that is 313. The two versions agree in substance but not in every phrase, since Eusebius's is a translation into Greek. The accounts of Constantine's sign differ: Lactantius tells of a dream before the battle with Maxentius, Eusebius of a cross of light seen in the sky on the march, as the emperor told it to him years later under oath. The date of the meeting at Milan is not given; Lactantius says only that Constantine went there about the beginning of winter.

people.name: St Constantine the Great
people.role: Emperor in the West; victor at the Milvian Bridge, who agreed the policy of religious freedom with Licinius at Milan.

people.name: Emperor Licinius
people.role: Constantine's colleague and brother-in-law; defeated Maximin and posted the agreement at Nicomedia in June 313.

people.name: Constantia
people.role: Constantine's sister, married to Licinius at Milan in the winter of the meeting.

people.name: Emperor Maxentius
people.role: Ruler of Rome, defeated by Constantine at the Milvian Bridge in October 312 and drowned in the Tiber.

people.name: Emperor Maximin Daia
people.role: Emperor in the East who renewed the persecution after 311; beaten by Licinius, he granted freedom before his death at Tarsus.

people.name: Lactantius
people.role: Christian writer; preserved the Latin text of the letter in On the Deaths of the Persecutors.

people.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
people.role: Bishop and historian; preserved the Greek text in his Church History and described the peace that followed.

review.basis: Rests on Lactantius's On the Deaths of the Persecutors (ANF vol. 7) and Eusebius's Church History and Life of Constantine (NPNF2 vol. 1), with Socrates for Licinius's later turn. Quotations are verbatim from those translations; the rest is our paraphrase.
